passage: In the colony park, the older boys pointed at the man who talked to himself near the gate. "Paagal! Paagal!" they chanted. Sunaina laughed too, then stopped. At night her own worries buzzed like mosquitoes and kept her awake. Would they call her paagal too? She decided never to tell anyone. Irfan Uncle from the second floor had heard the boys. That evening, watering his plants, he said, "That man's mind is unwell, the way a body gets unwell. It isn't funny, and it isn't his fault. I saw a doctor myself when my worries got too big." Sunaina twisted her frock. "Mine buzz at night," she whispered. Irfan Uncle put down the watering can. "Thank you for telling me. Let's go up and tell your Mummy together." They did, and Mummy hugged her and listened.

qa.q: What did the older boys chant?
qa.a: Paagal! Paagal!

qa.q: Why did Sunaina decide never to tell anyone about her night worries?
qa.a: After hearing the boys mock the man, she felt ashamed and feared they would call her paagal too.

qa.q: Which words from Irfan Uncle made it safe for Sunaina to speak?
qa.a: He said an unwell mind is like an unwell body, not funny and not anyone's fault, and that he too saw a doctor when his worries got too big.

qa.q: How might the man near the gate feel hearing the chant?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and ashamed, and less likely to reach out for help.

grounding: It shows a child learning from mockery that struggling is shameful, until an adult speaks openly about minds and health and she shares her own worries.

passage:
"Look at Kunal flapping his hands again. Something's wrong in his head!"
"Stop it. He's just excited about the rocket model."
"Tanuja, why are you taking his side? Are you weird too?"
Tanuja went quiet. She thought of how she checked her school bag five times every morning, and hid her hands under the desk.
Salma Ma'am put down the chalk. "Enough. Everyone's mind works a bit differently. Kunal shows happiness with his hands. Some of us worry a lot. Talking about minds is like talking about a cough. It's health, not a joke."
After the bell, Tanuja lingered. "Ma'am, I check my bag again and again, or I feel scared. Is something wrong in my head?"
"Thank you for telling me, Tanuja. It's nothing to be ashamed of. Shall we tell your mother together at pickup today?"
Tanuja nodded, and her shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What was Kunal excited about?
qa.a: The rocket model.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja hide her hands under the desk?
qa.a: After hearing Kunal mocked, she felt ashamed and afraid that her own habit of checking her bag would make her seem weird too.

qa.q: Which choice by Salma Ma'am helped Tanuja most after the bell?
qa.a: She thanked Tanuja, said it was nothing to be ashamed of, and offered to tell Tanuja's mother together at pickup that day.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel hearing Salma Ma'am say he shows happiness with his hands?
qa.a: He may feel understood and protected instead of laughed at.

grounding: It shows a child who hears a classmate with a difference mocked and starts hiding her own worries, until a teacher talks about minds as health and listens.

passage:
"Papa, Aryan in my class goes to a doctor for his mind. Everyone says he's paagal."
Kunal put down the newspaper. "Who says that?"
"Everyone. And Mehul said crying is for weak people." Ritu, nine, poked her rice. "So I won't tell anyone when I'm sad. Ever."
Kunal turned his chair to face her. "Ritu, when you broke your arm, did we hide it?"
"No, we went to the doctor."
"Minds can get hurt or sick too. Going to a doctor for it is brave, not paagal. I saw a counsellor once, after Dada died. It helped me a lot."
Ritu stared. "You did?"
"I did. And if you're ever sad, I want you to tell me."

qa.q: What did Mehul say about crying?
qa.a: He said crying is for weak people.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after hearing classmates call Aryan paagal?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of sadness and afraid, deciding never to tell anyone when she was sad.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that protected Ritu from hiding her pain?
qa.a: He compared mental health to a broken arm, shared that he saw a counsellor and invited her to tell him when she's sad.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt hearing Ritu say she'd never tell anyone?
qa.a: He likely felt concerned and protective, which is why he turned to face her and spoke openly.

grounding: Shows a child learning from mockery that struggling is shameful, and a parent who speaks openly about mental health to keep her from hiding pain.

passage: When I was ten, our neighbours called my uncle "paagal" because he saw a doctor for sadness. I'm Akash. I heard them laughing on the stairs. So when I started feeling scared every night about exams, I told nobody. I thought people would laugh at me too. Then our class teacher, Rehana Ma'am, did a lesson about feelings. She said, "Your heart and your mind both need looking after. I talk to a counsellor sometimes. That's normal." Everyone went quiet. After class I stayed back and told her about the nights. She thanked me and called my mother that afternoon. I still remember how light I felt walking home.

qa.q: What did the neighbours call Akash's uncle?
qa.a: They called him "paagal."

qa.q: Why did Akash tell nobody about feeling scared?
qa.a: Akash felt ashamed and afraid of being laughed at, after hearing neighbours mock the uncle.

qa.q: What did Rehana Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She spoke openly about minds needing care, shared that she talks to a counsellor, thanked Akash and called Akash's mother that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Rehana Ma'am have felt when Akash stayed back to talk?
qa.a: She was likely glad and caring, grateful that her lesson made it safe to speak.

grounding: Shows a child who learns from mockery that struggling is shameful, and a teacher whose openness about mental health helps the child stop hiding pain.

passage:
Class note, Year 5, Wednesday.
Today at lunch I overheard several children calling a boy with tics "mental" and "pagal." Kiran, sitting nearby, looked down and went quiet. Later, when Kiran seemed upset about a lost game, Kiran whispered to me, "If I cry, they'll say I'm weak or mad too."
This afternoon I held a short class talk. I said that minds can get unwell just like bodies, that seeing a doctor or counsellor is sensible, and that words like "pagal" hurt real people. I told them I go to the dentist and I've also talked to a counsellor, and both are normal. Afterwards Kiran told me about feeling worried at home. I thanked Kiran and will speak to the family tomorrow. — Tanuja

qa.q: What did the children call the boy with tics?
qa.a: They called him "mental" and "pagal."

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after hearing those words?
qa.a: Kiran felt ashamed and afraid of being called weak or mad for crying.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that protected Kiran from hiding pain?
qa.a: Tanuja spoke openly with the class about minds and bodies, shared personal experience with a counsellor and thanked Kiran for sharing.

qa.q: How might the boy with tics feel if the class stops using those words?
qa.a: The boy may feel safer and less hurt, no longer mocked for being different.

grounding: Shows a child who hears mockery of mental illness and learns struggling is shameful, and a teacher whose open talk about health helps the child share.

passage:
Wednesday
Today at recess Rohan pointed at Elizabeth talking to herself on the swing and said, "Paagal!" Everyone laughed. Then someone said her mummy goes to a mad doctor. Elizabeth ran to the washroom.
I didn't laugh. But my stomach hurt. Because last month I cried a lot at night and didn't tell anyone. Now I think if I tell, they'll call me paagal too.
At dinner Chachu said Anand Uncle is "weak in the head" because he went to a hospital for his worry. I didn't eat my roti.
Later, Amma came to my bed. She said feelings can get sick like a stomach can, and that she saw a counsellor after Nani died, and it helped. "No one in this house is paagal for being sad," she said.
So I told her about the crying. She hugged me and said we'd talk to someone together.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Rohan call Elizabeth at recess?
qa.a: "Paagal!"

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi's stomach hurt after recess?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt hurt and scared, and ashamed of the secret crying, fearing being called paagal too.

qa.q: How did Amma protect Lakshmi from hiding pain?
qa.a: By speaking openly about feelings as health, sharing her own counselling after Nani died, and saying no one is paagal for being sad.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel in the washroom?
qa.a: She probably feels humiliated and hurt that her mother's help became a joke.

grounding: Lakshmi hears classmates and family mock mental health struggles and learns to hide pain, until Amma speaks openly about feelings and health.
